idiom_name: one function per rule over a token array with closures (acorn shape)
implementation_notes: JavaScript's dynamic objects make the classic structure disappear: a token array (or a lexer with a next method) plus one function per rule is the whole parser, with closures or module-scope helpers for peek/advance/expect and a SyntaxError (or a result object) for errors - acorn, the de-facto JavaScript parser, is exactly this shape. What replaces the classic structure is the language itself: no token class hierarchy, no visitor, no tables, and object literals used only for AST nodes. Keep this form when the grammar is small, the parser must run dependency-free in a browser or edge runtime, and precise error positions and recovery are required; choose the chevrotain variant when the grammar is bigger and a declarative LL(k) rule language with built-in lookahead, validation and recovery is worth a dependency.
pitfalls: JavaScript engines do not implement proper tail calls: recursion depth is bounded by the engine stack, so untrusted input needs an explicit depth guard; the failure signal is RangeError: Maximum call stack size exceeded.
Regex-based lexing with a shared /g regex carries lastIndex state; a lexer that forgets to reset it, or reuses one global regex in two places, produces position-dependent bugs.
Throwing SyntaxError on the first mismatch is idiomatic but loses recovery; tooling that needs multiple diagnostics must collect errors and synthesise nodes instead.

variants.name: Chevrotain LL(k) grammar
variants.idiom_name: chevrotain token vocabulary + rule methods with computed lookahead
variants.implementation_notes: Chevrotain is a parser building toolkit with built-in LL(k) support: token types are declared once as a vocabulary, every grammar rule is a method that consumes tokens and calls sub-rules, and performSelfAnalysis computes lookahead functions, validates the grammar and provides error recovery with a positioned CST - all in plain JavaScript, with no code generation. Prefer it when the grammar is large enough that lookahead must be managed mechanically and when grammar validation plus recovery matter (HyperFormula, Langium and JHipster JDL are production users); the cost is a dependency and a rule API to learn.
pitfalls: performSelfAnalysis must run once per parser class, not per parse; a second call throws, and calling it before all RULE properties are assigned produces confusing lookahead errors.

The grammar is validated against the token vocabulary, so an ambiguous or left-recursive rule fails at analysis time - useful, but it means the grammar must be LL(k) or refactored with explicit lookahead.
